title: Designing loud interfaces that still respect the user
description: Loud and usable aren't opposites. The trick is deciding — ruthlessly — what gets to shout, and making everything else stand at parade rest.
author: Marlo Vane
imageAlt: A poster wall of loud typographic experiments
content:
Every few months a client says the same sentence to me: we want it bold, but not too much. What they're really asking is whether loudness and usability are enemies. They aren't — but the peace treaty has terms.

Loudness is a budget

A page can afford roughly one scream, two raised voices, and unlimited murmurs. The scream is your headline or your accent block. The raised voices are section openers and primary actions. Everything else — body copy, borders, metadata — should be set at conversational volume so the loud parts land.

The failure mode isn't boldness. It's uniform boldness: when everything is capitalised, boxed, and pink, nothing is. Brutalism without hierarchy is just noise with a grid.

Three rules I actually follow

  • One sticker per viewport. A rotated pill, a hard shadow, a marquee — pick one per screenful and let it own the moment.
  • Hairlines are free, fills are expensive. Ink borders give structure without weight. A filled block is a spent bullet; make it count.
  • Type does the acting, layout does the directing. If a layout trick and a type choice can achieve the same emphasis, choose type — it survives every screen size.
Loud design isn't the absence of restraint. It's restraint spent all in one place.

Respect is in the defaults

The quiet parts are where users learn to trust you: honest focus states, real contrast ratios, motion that respects the reduced-motion flag, tap targets sized for thumbs and not for mockups. Get those boringly right and you've earned the right to be weird everywhere else.

That's the whole trade. Discipline underneath, mischief on top.

title: Brutalism is a budget decision
description: The style everyone calls a trend is actually the cheapest honest design language on the web — if you understand what it's spending instead.
author: Marlo Vane
imageAlt: Ink rules and stacked type on cream paper
content:
Web brutalism gets written up as an aesthetic rebellion. Sure. But strip the think-pieces away and you find something more practical underneath: it's the design language that spends money where users can feel it.

What the style refuses to buy

No stock photography of people laughing at salads. No gradient meshes rendered in someone's GPU farm. No icon set that needs a licensing call. A brutalist page is type, rules, and honest color — assets you already own the moment you can write a sentence.

Where the budget actually goes

Into the words. A page with nothing to hide behind lives or dies on its copy, so you finally pay for good copy. Into the type — one great family beats six mediocre ones and costs less. And into speed: pages built from text and borders are light by construction. My last three launches shipped under 90KB before fonts. Nobody's gradient mesh does that.

A style that can't hide bad thinking forces good thinking. That's not a constraint — that's the product.

The honest caveat

Brutalism is cheap to build and expensive to fake. Because there's no decoration to absorb error, a sloppy brutalist page looks broken rather than boring. The rules have to be exact, the spacing deliberate, the hierarchy airtight. You're not spending less craft — you're spending it where it shows.

Which, if you ask me, is the only place worth spending it.

title: The tools I actually open in 2026
description: Ignore the stack screenshots. Here's the short, honest list of what survives daily use in a one-person studio — and what quietly got uninstalled.
author: Marlo Vane
imageAlt: A tidy desk with one monitor, one notebook, one coffee
content:
Every January the tool-stack posts bloom: forty apps, twelve subscriptions, a workflow diagram that looks like a subway map. Here's mine instead — the things I opened yesterday, because that's the only endorsement that means anything.

The daily five

  • A design tool — for exactly two jobs: moving rectangles until the idea shows up, and handing clients something they can point at. Final decisions happen in the browser.
  • A code editor with an agent in it — the single biggest change to my practice in a decade. It writes the boilerplate; I keep the taste.
  • A plain-text notes file — one file, one year, searchable. Every fancier system I've tried was a procrastination scheme with sync.
  • A time tracker — not for billing theatre, but because pricing improves when you stop lying to yourself about hours.
  • Email — the whole CRM. If a relationship can't survive in an inbox, a kanban board won't save it.

What got uninstalled

The whiteboard app nobody else ever joined. The project manager that was really a guilt machine with swimlanes. Three AI image tools that produced the same purple robot. The rule that emerged: if a tool needs a habit built around it, the tool is the problem.

Your stack is not your studio. The work is the studio.

Ask what you'd keep if every subscription doubled in price tomorrow. That list is your actual stack. Mine fits in one hand.

title: How I price creative work without hating myself
description: Day rates punish speed, value pricing rewards theatre. After twelve years I landed on something simpler: price the decision, not the hours.
author: Marlo Vane
imageAlt: A printed proposal with a single bold number circled in pink
content:
Nobody teaches you pricing. You graduate knowing kerning and nothing about the moment a founder asks what does something like this cost? and your mouth goes dry. Twelve years in, here's the system that finally stopped the dread.

Why the standard models chafe

Hourly billing punishes you for getting good — the faster you are, the less you earn. Pure value pricing sounds right in the podcast and collapses in the meeting, because computing the lifetime value of a rebrand is astrology with spreadsheets. Both models make the conversation about you — your hours, your worth — when it should be about the decision the client is buying.

Price the decision

Every engagement I take is one of three decisions, and each has a floor:

  • Direction — which way should this brand or product point? Workshops, strategy, one loud recommendation.
  • Definition — what exactly are we making? Identity systems, design systems, the site architecture.
  • Delivery — make it real and ship it. Design plus build, end to end.

Clients pick the decision they need; the price is attached to the decision, not the hours behind it. Scope talks get shorter because we're negotiating meaning, not minutes.

A price is a claim about consequences. Charge for what the work changes, not for what it takes out of you.

The three rules that hold it together

First: never price in the room. Enthusiasm is a discount you pay for later. Second: every proposal has exactly one number — options create haggling, one number creates a yes or a useful no. Third: raise the floor every third project. If nobody has winced in six months, you're subsidising someone's Series A.

I still get the dry mouth sometimes. But now it's before the email, not before the invoice.
